extracted.intended_audience: affective neuroscientists, cognitive neuroscientists, neuropsychologists, and researchers studying reward/pleasure in humans and animals
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly review synthesizing human and animal research on neural mechanisms of pleasure and reward, emphasizing distinctions among psychological components (liking, wanting, learning), methods to infer coding vs causation, hedonic hotspots, and translational implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liking
rubrics_metrics.description: “the actual pleasure component or hedonic impact of a reward. Pleasure comprises two levels: (1) core ‘liking’ reactions that need not necessarily be conscious; (2) conscious experiences of pleasure, in the ordinary sense of the word, which may be elaborated out of core ‘liking’ reactions by cognitive brain mechanisms of awareness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both behavioral/objective measures (e.g., species-homologous facial ‘liking’ reactions to sweet tastes) and subjective reports where possible; distinguish core non-conscious ‘liking’ from conscious subjective pleasure when interpreting data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wanting
rubrics_metrics.description: “motivation for reward, which includes both (1) incentive salience ‘wanting’ processes that are not necessarily conscious and (2) conscious desires for incentives or cognitive goals.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat incentive-salience processes (often dopamine-related) separately from hedonic impact; experimental designs should dissociate motivational drive from hedonic pleasure (e.g., measures of cue-triggered approach vs. facial ‘liking’).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning
rubrics_metrics.description: “associations, representations, and predictions about future rewards based on past experiences. Learned predictions include both (1) explicit and cognitive predictions and (2) implicit knowledge as well as associative conditioning, such as basic Pavlovian and instrumental associations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure associative and predictive processes (e.g., prediction error signals, Pavlovian/instrumental conditioning) separately from immediate hedonic and motivational measures; include both explicit and implicit assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish neural coding from neural causation
rubrics_metrics.description: “A useful distinction can be made between coding and causing pleasure in the brain: coding is inferred by measuring brain activity correlated to a pleasure (PET, fMRI, MEG, electrophysiology), whereas causation is inferred on the basis of a change in pleasure as a consequence of a brain manipulation such as lesion or stimulation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that a region whose activity correlates with pleasure necessarily generates it. Combine correlational neuroimaging with causal manipulations (lesions, pharmacology, stimulation) to support claims of causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary versus sufficient causes of pleasure (experimental approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Necessary causation: ask ‘What reward function is lost?’ when a brain system is suppressed (lesion, antagonist, genetic manipulation). Sufficient causation: activate a system (agonist, stimulation) and ask whether reward occurs or is magnified.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design both loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments to test necessity and sufficiency; be aware they need not co-occur (a region can be sufficient without being necessary and vice versa). Example: nucleus accumbens activation can be sufficient to enhance reward though lesions may only subtly impair natural hedonic impact; posterior ventral pallidum lesions can abolish ‘liking’.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective versus subjective measures of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: “Pleasure has manifestations both in consciousness (subjective liking) and in brain and behavioral reactions (objective ‘liking’). While subjective reports measure conscious pleasure in humans, objective ‘liking’ reactions (e.g., affective facial expressions to tastes) provide a cross-species handle for hedonic impact.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine subjective ratings (when available) with objective behavioral/physiological markers (facial expressions, orofacial reactions, neuronal firing patterns) to triangulate hedonic impact, especially in translational animal–human comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for identifying hedonic hotspots
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hedonic hotspots are small localized regions (e.g., cubic millimeter in rodents) in structures such as nucleus accumbens shell, ventral pallidum, and parabrachial nucleus where opioid or endocannabinoid stimulation causes amplification of core ‘liking’ reactions to sweetness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence for a hotspot should include: localized microinjection or stimulation that doubles/triples ‘liking’ reactions to palatable stimuli; anatomical specificity (not broad arousal); enhancement occurs only when palatable stimulus is present; signature pattern of hedonic behavioral responses; ideally converging neuronal coding data. Consider hierarchical/heterarchical interactions (multiple hotspots may need to cooperate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules to rule out general arousal or non-hedonic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: “Objective evidence for ‘liking’ enhancement needs special scrutiny to ensure that a brain activation does not merely cause something simpler, such as general arousal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control tests should show that activation: (a) does not amplify negative ‘disliking’ or neutral reactions, (b) only enhances hedonic reactions when a palatable stimulus is present, (c) produces a signature hedonic pattern rather than indiscriminate motor activation. Use converging measures (behavioral pattern, neuronal firing specificity) to exclude arousal explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective (sensory-specific) satiety as a method to track reward value
rubrics_metrics.description: “Selective or sensory-specific satiety (reinforcer devaluation) compares responses to food-related stimuli when hungry and after eating to satiety on one food; mid-anterior orbitofrontal cortex activity tracks changes in reward value of the food eaten to satiety.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selective satiety manipulations to dissociate sensory intensity from hedonic valuation; expect orbitofrontal activity to decrease selectively for the sated food while remaining for other foods, correlating with subjective pleasantness changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-conscious hedonic processes in definitions and measures
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hedonic reactions themselves can actually even be non-conscious. Non-conscious ‘liking’ and ‘wanting’ without subjective awareness has been produced in ordinary people (e.g., subliminal exposure to emotional faces altering consumption and ventral pallidum/amygdala activation).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies to detect unconscious hedonic influences (subliminal priming, physiological/neural markers) and avoid equating pleasure solely with conscious feeling; this allows better translation between animal core ‘liking’ and human subjective pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-species homology as translational evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Homologous affective expressions (e.g., neonatal facial ‘liking’ to sweetness) shared across species imply underlying hedonic brain mechanisms are similar, opening the way for affective neuroscience of pleasure that bridges humans and animals.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use homologous behavioral markers (timing, pattern) and conserved neural circuits to justify translational claims; nonetheless, account for higher-order cognitive elaboration in humans that may qualitatively differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orbitofrontal cortex as key locus for subjective hedonic coding (but limited causal claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Converging findings indicate the human orbitofrontal cortex (especially mid-anterior OFC) correlates with subjective pleasantness ratings and may be an important nexus for sensory integration, emotional processing, and hedonic experience; however, cortical causation of pleasure requires closer scrutiny.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use OFC activity correlations (fMRI/MEG) and manipulations (e.g., DBS with MEG readouts) to link OFC to subjective experience, but complement correlational data with causal interventions and network-level analyses given that cortex may code without being the primary generator of core ‘liking’.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four computational principles for sensory–hedonic interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Four computational principles proposed for the interaction between sensory and hedonic processing in humans and other primates: (1) motivation-independent processing of identity and intensity, (2) formation of learning-dependent multimodal sensory representations, (3) reward representations using state-dependent mechanisms including selective satiation, and (4) representations of hedonic experience, monitoring/learning, or direct behavioral change.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling or interpreting sensory–hedonic interactions, ensure experimental designs and analyses consider these principles (separate identity/intensity coding, include learning/multimodal representations, account for state-dependence, and link representational measures to hedonic/behavioral outcomes).
